texas-guard-ah64e-apaches-jbsa-lackland.content:
The first three AH-64E Apache attack helicopters assigned to the Texas Army National Guard's 1st Battalion, 149th Aviation Regiment touched down at Kelly Field, Joint Base San Antonio-Lackland, on Sept. 24, 2026, opening a months-long relocation that folds the Guard battalion into one of the Army's most contested force-structure overhauls in decades.

The move places the 1-149th — a National Guard reconnaissance battalion under the 36th Combat Aviation Brigade, 36th Infantry Division — at Kelly Field as part of what the Army calls its reformatting plan, the service's broad effort to reshape aviation around fewer, more modern aircraft.

For the battalion, the relocation is the second phase of a transformation that began in February. On Feb. 3, 2026, the 1st Battalion, 101st Aviation Regiment — the active-duty "No Mercy" battalion at Fort Campbell, Kentucky — transferred its first two AH-64E Apache Version 4 helicopters to the Texas and Mississippi Guards, with the 1-149th receiving the airframes as the 101st made room for the incoming Version 6 upgrade.

Lt. Col. Cody Anfinson, the 1-149th's commander, described the handover as a milestone for a unit with long Apache roots. The battalion retired the last AH-64A in the entire Army back in July 2012 — tail number 90-00451, flown out of Ellington Field in Houston — and has waited more than a decade to step into the Army's latest attack helicopter.

## A Guard battalion at the center of Army reform

The relocation lands the 1-149th squarely in the middle of the Army Transformation Initiative, launched by a Pentagon memo in April 2025 and now being executed across the aviation branch. Under the plan, the active-duty AH-64E fleet is shrinking from 408 airframes to 240, with the newest helicopters transferring into the National Guard. Eleven active air cavalry squadrons and two reserve expeditionary combat aviation brigades are being disbanded, older AH-64D models are being decommissioned outright, and roughly 6,500 aviation positions are being cut across 2026 and 2027, according to figures reported by Aviation Week and cited by Defense Express.

Army leaders have framed the cuts as a trade: fewer helicopters, but newer ones, concentrated where they can be sustained. The Guard, with its deep maintenance experience, is being positioned as the long-term home for the Apache even as the active force pivots toward unmanned systems and next-generation aircraft.

The 1-149th's structure reflects the Guard model. Its headquarters sits at Ellington Field Joint Reserve Base in Houston; Company A belongs to the Mississippi Army National Guard, while Companies B and C are Texas units. Consolidating the battalion at Kelly Field brings its aircraft, maintainers, and crews under one roof at an installation with deep aviation roots — Kelly Field has launched military aircraft for more than a century.

## Version 4 today, Version 6 tomorrow

The helicopters arriving in San Antonio are AH-64E Version 4 aircraft, the configuration the 101st is shedding as it converts to Version 6 — a standard that brings improved rotor blades, larger fuel capacity, and a large-area cockpit display, according to Boeing. For a Guard battalion that flew the oldest Apaches in the Army just over a decade ago, the Version 4 aircraft represent a generational jump in sensors, networking, and lethality.

The relocation is expected to take months to complete as aircraft, equipment, and personnel flow south from the battalion's current stations. When finished, the 1-149th will be one of the Guard's most modern attack battalions — and a test case for the Army's bet that the National Guard can carry a larger share of the service's attack aviation future.

osprey-mv22b-sonobuoy-asw-test.content:
An MV-22B Osprey dropped sonobuoys over the Pacific off San Clemente Island, California, on Aug. 19, 2026, completing the first lot acceptance test of the sensors from a tiltrotor — a milestone the Navy says could reshape how it keeps its undersea surveillance inventory honest.

The test brought together the Air Anti-Submarine Warfare Systems Program Office (PMA-264), the V-22 Joint Program Office (PMA-275), and Marine Operational Test and Evaluation Squadron 1 (VMX-1), flying an aircraft out of Marine Corps Air Station Miramar. It was announced Sept. 22 by PMA-264 and detailed in a Defense Department release the following day.

The mission was not a combat exercise. It was an acceptance run for the Navy's Sonobuoy Quality Assurance Program, which pulls random production samples of sonobuoys and drops them over water to verify reliability and acoustic performance before the lots reach operational squadrons. Until now, that job belonged to the P-3C Orions of Air Test and Evaluation Squadron 30 (VX-30), using automated cockpit-triggered launchers.

## Manual drops from the ramp

The Osprey did it the hard way. With the rear cargo ramp open, crew chiefs manually removed the buoys' container caps and inverted the launch tubes into the slipstream — a hands-on evolution a world away from the P-3's push-button dispensers. Defense Department photographs show the loading and rigging work at Miramar in the days before the flight.

Navy Capt. Greg Hinkle, PMA-264's program manager, said the focus of the quality assurance program is making sure the sonobuoys delivered to the fleet perform exactly as expected, and that using the Osprey for the mission reinforces the supply chain and ensures front-line aircrews have mission-ready stores to detect and track undersea threats.

The test gives the Navy a dependable substitute if its primary test platforms are unavailable, preventing backlogs in the acceptance pipeline as the P-3C fleet winds down.


The test crew came from VMX-1, the Marine Corps' operational test squadron at Miramar — the same community that wrings out every new Marine aircraft before it reaches the fleet. Their involvement signals that the Navy views the Osprey not as a one-off test mule but as a standing member of the sonobuoy enterprise.

There is precedent. A 2025 photograph from the Philippine Sea showed a VMM-265 crew chief handling sonobuoys aboard an Osprey with the 31st Marine Expeditionary Unit — evidence that the fleet has been quietly working the problem for at least a year. The August test formalized it: the tiltrotor is now a validated, dependable substitute in the quality-assurance chain, the backstop that keeps acceptance testing moving when the P-3Cs are down or tasked elsewhere.

## A door left open

The official release frames the event as laying the groundwork for expanded tactical employment across the fleet — careful language that stops short of declaring the Osprey an operational submarine hunter. But the implications are hard to miss. A tiltrotor that can sprint to a datum far faster than a helicopter and then slow to work a contact has obvious appeal for anti-submarine warfare, and Marine crews have been experimenting at the margins for years: a 2025 photograph showed a VMM-265 crew chief handling sonobuoys in the Philippine Sea.

For now, the verified achievement is narrower and arguably more important: the supply chain that feeds the fleet's ears in the water has a new, faster backup. In a Pacific where submarines are the pacing threat, that is not a small thing.

sea-drone-rescued-apache-crew-saronic.content:
Secretary of War Pete Hegseth stood on the factory floor of Saronic Technologies in Austin, Texas, on Sept. 18, 2026, and called the startup "the gold standard" of American military manufacturing. He had a story to tell about why.

Three months earlier, on June 8, a U.S. Army AH-64 Apache patrolling over the Strait of Hormuz went down off the coast of Oman after taking Iranian fire — President Donald Trump later confirmed that Iran had shot the helicopter down. The two crew members ended up in the water, roughly two hours from help, in airspace too dangerous for a manned rescue helicopter.

The Navy sent a boat with no crew at all.

The vessel was a Corsair, a 24-foot autonomous surface vessel built by Saronic and operated by the 5th Fleet's Task Force 59, the Navy's unmanned-systems experimentation unit. It reached the downed aviators, who hauled themselves aboard, then moved them to a second location because of what U.S. Central Command described as operational circumstances. From there a helicopter hoisted them out. Both crew members were reported stable.

Defense officials believe it was the first known personnel recovery ever carried out by an unmanned surface vessel.

## The "Arsenal of Freedom" tour

Hegseth's Austin stop was part of a swing he branded the "Arsenal of Freedom" tour, aimed at showcasing the commercial shipyards and startups the Pentagon wants to pull into its industrial base. Saronic's chief executive, Dino Mavrookas, introduced him, and the secretary used the visit to promise fast contracts for companies that deliver — and the door for those that don't.

The Corsair that made the pickup is no prototype. The 24-foot boat tops 35 knots, ranges 1,000 nautical miles, and carries a 1,000-pound payload. Saronic says it went from prototype to serial production of 300 hulls in under a year, backed by a $392 million late-2025 production contract and a $1.75 billion funding round in March 2026. The company is also building "Port Alpha," a $3.2 billion shipyard in South Texas whose first phase is expected to be operational by 2028.

## Why a robot boat

The rescue's backstory explains the decision. The Apache was one of at least seven crewed U.S. aircraft lost to Iranian fire since February 2026, during the U.S.-Iran conflict that began with Operation Epic Fury. Sending a manned helicopter into the same airspace to hover over survivors was judged too risky; the unmanned boat could go where crews could not.

CENTCOM said the operation was run by Naval Forces Central Command with the 82nd Airborne Division, and spokesman Capt. Tim Hawkins confirmed the Corsair's role to DefenseScoop. Saronic co-founder Rob Lehman later walked through the mission on a DefenseScoop podcast, describing a vessel designed for exactly this kind of dull, dangerous work.

The Pentagon has not said whether the Corsair's rescue will become doctrine. But on a factory floor in Austin, the secretary of war treated it as a preview — of a fleet where the first responder to a downed crew might not have a crew at all.

us-panama-k1000-drones-6-million.content:
The United States handed Panama four long-range K1000 surveillance drones on Sept. 16, 2026, a package worth more than $6 million aimed at pushing the fight against drug trafficking and human smuggling farther from American shores.

U.S. Ambassador Kevin Marino Cabrera delivered the aircraft to Panama's Ministry of Public Security at a ceremony at Lieutenant Octavio Rodríguez Garrido Air Base in Panama Pacifico, with Panamanian Security Minister Frank Ábrego in attendance. The package was funded by U.S. Southern Command.

The drones will be flown by Panama's National Aeronaval Service, known as Senan, to monitor remote borders and safeguard strategic maritime corridors, according to the U.S. Embassy in Panama. The stated mission set: dismantling drug trafficking and human smuggling networks, and halting transnational threats long before they approach American soil — the embassy's own headline framed the delivery as protecting the American homeland.

## Pilots trained, then handed the keys

The handover doubled as a graduation. Ten newly certified Panamanian drone pilots received their qualifications the same day, completing a six-week, U.S.-funded training program led by Kraus Hamdani Aerospace, the American company that builds the K1000.

Cabrera tied the delivery to the administration's broader push, saying that under President Trump's leadership the United States is driving expanded security cooperation with Panama through concrete, results-oriented investments, and that scaling up joint capabilities on land and at sea is aimed at aggressively stopping transnational threats at the source.


The ceremony itself drew local attention. Abrego left a National Assembly budget session early to attend, a move that drew questions from opposition deputy Jonathan Vega, according to Panamanian outlet conven.org — a reminder that American security assistance, however welcome, is never politically free.

Senan, the recipient service, is Panama's combined air-and-sea arm, responsible for patrolling the country's long Pacific and Caribbean coastlines and the remote jungle border regions where smugglers move drugs north and migrants south. Persistent aerial surveillance has been the missing piece: Panama's forces have long relied on tip-offs and patrol craft, arriving after the fact. A drone that can watch a coastline for a full day changes that equation.

## A 45-pound workhorse

The K1000 is built for endurance rather than firepower. The 45-pound aircraft spans 16.4 feet, cruises up to 75 mph, and can stay aloft 24 hours in its solar-recharge configuration — 12 hours in vertical-takeoff mode — with a range of about 1,000 miles. It operates line-of-sight within 90 miles or beyond line-of-sight via satellite, and a three-person crew can unpack it from Pelican cases and have it flying in under 15 minutes.

That combination — long legs, tiny logistics footprint, no runway — is what makes it suited to Panama's geography: dense jungle borders, long coastlines, and the maritime corridors threading toward the canal.

The delivery landed amid a wider Pentagon shift. CNN has reported the Defense Department moving MQ-9 Reaper drones from Africa to Southern Command's area of responsibility, alongside months of U.S. strikes on alleged drug traffickers in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific. The K1000s give Panama its own persistent eye in the sky — American-funded, American-trained, but Panamanian-flown.

uss-george-washington-200000th-aircraft.content:
An F-35C Lightning II caught the number three wire aboard USS George Washington on Aug. 18, 2026, and made history doing it: the 200,000th fixed-wing aircraft recovery in the carrier's 34 years at sea.

The milestone trap happened as the ship steamed in the Indian Ocean. The pilot was Lt. Steven Frazier of Strike Fighter Squadron 147, the "Argonauts," flying a routine sortie in the U.S. 7th Fleet area of operations.

Rear Adm. Jeffrey L. Heames, commander of Carrier Strike Group 5, called the number a testament to the enduring strength of American naval aviation and the professionalism of the sailors who make it possible, adding that U.S. carriers remain ready to launch and recover aircraft anywhere, anytime.

## Thirty-four years of traps

George Washington was commissioned on July 4, 1992 — the sixth Nimitz-class carrier — and has been the Navy's only permanently forward-deployed carrier, homeported in Japan, since 2008. The aircraft it has recovered trace the evolution of naval aviation itself: F-14 Tomcats in the 1990s, legacy F/A-18 Hornets, then Super Hornets, EA-18G Growlers, E-2 Hawkeyes, and now the F-35C.

A trap is a violent, precise event. The aircraft snags a steel arresting cable with its tailhook at more than 140 miles per hour; a carrier at full tempo can land one aircraft per minute, roughly 70 a day. Two hundred thousand of them represents decades of flight-deck crews working in one of the most dangerous industrial environments on earth.

"For the George Washington, more than anything, it shows consistency over the last 34 years to be able to complete whatever mission the country calls upon it to do," Frazier said. "For me personally, it shows that if this aircraft carrier launches me off of the ship, I'll be able to come back and land on it."

The milestone also quietly underlines the durability of the Nimitz design. While the newer Ford class has wrestled with its launch and recovery systems, George Washington's counter kept turning — 200,000 recoveries without fanfare, on a hull commissioned when the Soviet Union had been gone barely seven months.


George Washington is the flagship of Carrier Strike Group 5, the Navy's only permanently forward-deployed strike group, homeported at Yokosuka, Japan. The 200,000th trap is as much a tribute to the ship's company — the catapult and arresting-gear crews, the ordnancemen, the controllers in the tower — as to the pilots. A carrier's trap count is the one statistic that cannot be spun: every number on that board was a real airplane, a real deck, a real wire.

## Straight into the fight

The celebration was brief. The ship's 7th Fleet patrol had already kept it at sea for months; the Arabian Sea tasking extended that deployment into one of the longest continuous forward operations of the carrier's career.

Two days after the milestone, George Washington sailed into the Arabian Sea to take over the Middle East mission from USS Abraham Lincoln, whose marathon deployment — including combat operations against Iran — was ending. The move left a temporary carrier gap in the Western Pacific, a trade the Navy accepted to keep pressure on in the Central Command theater.

aim260-jatm-australian-super-hornet.content:
A U.S. Navy photograph released Sept. 30, 2026, shows something airpower watchers have waited years to see clearly: an inert AIM-260 Joint Advanced Tactical Missile riding the cheek station of an Australian F/A-18F Super Hornet.

The image, taken Sept. 11 by Navy photographer Dana Rene White, captures the Royal Australian Air Force jet — assigned to No. 1 Squadron — taking off from Naval Base Ventura County Point Mugu in California during Gray Flag 2026, the Navy's sprawling test exercise. The missile's blue bands mark it as an inert round: no live rocket motor, no warhead.

The loadout tells its own story. Alongside the AIM-260, the jet carried inert CATM-9X and CATM-120 training rounds, three external fuel tanks, an AN/ASQ-228 ATFLIR targeting pod, and a Tactical Combat Training System pod — a test configuration, not a war load.

## Australia's $480 million bet

The sighting came weeks after Australia announced in August 2026 that it would buy the AIM-260 through U.S. Foreign Military Sales, becoming the first country outside the United States to operate the missile. The deal is valued at roughly $480 million — reported in Australia as almost 736 million Australian dollars — with RAAF Super Hornets first in line, followed by the F-35A and the EA-18G Growler. The MQ-28 Ghost Bat has been named as a possible future candidate.

Canberra's own language was measured: the acquisition, Australia said, will give its air force a credible deterrent against airborne targets, complementing existing air-to-air missile capabilities. No delivery timeline has been disclosed.

## The missile meant to outrange the threat

The AIM-260, built by Lockheed Martin under a program the Pentagon launched in 2017, is designed to outrange the AIM-120 AMRAAM it will eventually succeed — prior reporting puts its reach at 120 miles or more — while keeping a similar form factor so it fits the internal weapons bays of the F-22 and F-35. Its development has been paced by China's PL-15, the very-long-range missile carried by the J-20.

The program is accelerating. In September 2026 the Pentagon and Lockheed Martin signed a framework agreement to push production and multiyear procurement, and the Air Force Test Center has confirmed both ground and airborne testing. The first-ever public photo of a U.S. AIM-260 appeared only in May 2026, on a VX-31 test jet at Eglin Air Force Base in Florida — making the Australian sighting the second public glimpse, and the first involving a foreign operator.

Gray Flag itself was the largest to date: more than 3,000 personnel, 150 organizations, 750 sorties, and 2,000 flight hours flown from the Point Mugu Sea Range.


The missile sighting is part of a wider U.S.-Australian air-weapons partnership. RAAF Super Hornets are also involved in the Hypersonic Attack Cruise Missile effort under the Southern Cross Integrated Flight Research Experiment, or SCIFiRE — a separate program, but evidence of how deeply the two air forces have intertwined their long-range strike planning.

One caution from the analysts who first published the photo: it does not establish whether the missile was Australian-owned, a U.S. test asset, or part of a specific integration effort. What it does establish is that the West's next long-range air-to-air missile is now flying on allied jets — inert for now, in public for the first time.

ukraine-f16-fleet-readiness-crisis.content:
More than half of Ukraine's donated F-16 fighters are stuck in what a Western official calls "maintenance limbo," and at the current pace Kyiv could exhaust its remaining available aircraft by the end of 2026, the Wall Street Journal reported on Sept. 30, 2026.

The Ukrainian Air Force declined to give the Journal fleet-status figures, so the assessment rests on Western sources — but Reuters independently confirmed the core of it on Oct. 8, reporting that many of the donated jets are back in western Europe for repairs, grounded by a lack of engine parts.

## The maintenance bottleneck

Ukraine has received an estimated 40 to 50 F-16s, with some airframes held back in Europe for training and five confirmed lost in combat. Another 110 have been pledged by Belgium, Denmark, the Netherlands, and Norway. The problem is not just airframes — it is the pipeline that keeps them flying.

Long-term maintenance is done in Belgium by Sabena Aerospace Engineering, where phase inspections are taking up to 40 weeks — against two to six weeks in the United States. For a fleet flying daily combat air-defense sorties, that math is brutal.

The timing could hardly be worse. Ukraine's F-16s have become workhorses of the air-defense campaign, thrown against Russian cruise missiles and, increasingly, Russia's new jet-powered Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones. Analyst Michael Kofman has noted the Vipers playing an important role in those intercepts — the kind of grinding, unglamorous work that eats airframes.

## Running low on missiles

The jets are also running out of things to shoot. AIM-9 Sidewinders and AIM-120 AMRAAMs have been expended in large numbers against incoming missiles and drones, and the same AMRAAMs feed Ukraine's NASAMS ground-based air-defense batteries — two hungers drawing from one stockpile.

Ukrainian pilots are rationing missile shots and falling back on the F-16's internal 20mm M61A1 Vulcan cannon, with Kyiv negotiating for tens of thousands of additional 20mm rounds. It is a measure of the strain: a fourth-generation fighter reduced to gun runs because the missile pipeline cannot keep up.


The sustainment problem starts long before the flight line. Ukrainian pilots and maintainers trained in the United States, Denmark, and Romania on compressed timelines, and the maintenance culture they entered is unforgiving: an F-16 is a maintenance-hungry aircraft even in peacetime, a demand that only grows under combat tempo and dispersed basing. Spare engines, avionics boxes, and structural parts were always the long poles of the fleet — and they are now the poles that are breaking.

## A fleet pressed into a different war

The donated Vipers are older European mid-life-update airframes, pledged for air combat and strike missions. Instead they have been pressed into the air-defense grind — a role that burns through engines, parts, and missiles at a rate no peacetime sustainment plan contemplated.

Reuters framed the wider picture bluntly: Ukraine has, in essence, run out of the air-defense missiles that matter most. The F-16 fleet's troubles are one front in a broader air-defense crisis — one that Western capitals, well into the war's fourth year, have not solved. With winter approaching and Russia's drone and missile campaign showing no sign of easing, the pressure on the remaining flyable jets will only grow.

vfa41-epic-fury-weapons-expended.content:
A single Navy fighter squadron fired 421 missiles and bombs during Operation Epic Fury — and someone kept count.

A photograph of VFA-41's expenditure board, shared by aviation photographer Jeff Rojas, lays out the "Black Aces'" full wartime bill from the U.S. air campaign against Iran: 173 GBU-38 500-pound JDAMs, 52 GBU-31(V)4 bunker-buster 2,000-pounders, 48 dual-mode laser JDAMs, 41 JSOW glide bombs, 33 AIM-9X Sidewinders, 30 standard 2,000-pound JDAMs, 27 1,000-pound JDAMs, 10 SLAM-ER cruise missiles, 6 AIM-120 AMRAAMs, and a single GBU-12 laser-guided bomb.

The War Zone, which first published the tally, estimates the ordnance cost at roughly $43.6 million at minimum — derived from U.S. military budget documents, with the caveat that munitions pricing fluctuates and JDAM kit costs are hard to separate from the warheads they guide.

## Two months of war

VFA-41 flies the F/A-18F Super Hornet as part of the air wing aboard USS Abraham Lincoln. The Pentagon says Operation Epic Fury ran from Feb. 28 to May 5, 2026 — about nine weeks — though American strikes on Iranian targets continued intermittently afterward. Lincoln, on a marathon deployment stretching back to 2025, had just left the Middle East when the tally surfaced in early October, bound for home in San Diego.

The air-to-air portion of the list is its own story. Thirty-three AIM-9Xs and six AMRAAMs with no known kills of crewed Iranian aircraft — the missiles were almost certainly fired at Iranian drones, and possibly cruise missiles. After a crash program in 2024, Super Hornets can now carry up to nine air-to-air missiles per sortie, a configuration crews call the "Murder Hornet" loadout, built specifically for the drone threat.


The expenditure has reignited Washington's munitions debate. Precision weapons take years to build and cannot be surged overnight; Pentagon planners have warned for years that a high-end fight would burn through stockpiles faster than industry can replace them. Epic Fury — nine weeks, one squadron, 421 weapons — is now the freshest data point in that argument. Multiply the Black Aces' bill across Lincoln's four strike squadrons, the rest of the joint force, and the months of intermittent strikes that followed, and the industrial question answers itself.

## Markings of a drone war

The squadron's jets came home decorated. One VFA-41 Super Hornet, Bureau Number 168491, returned to Naval Air Station Lemoore on Oct. 1 with a broken-submarine silhouette painted under the cockpit labeled "Sub Buster" — believed to mark a kill on an Iranian submarine, a first for the type. Iranian Kilo-class and Ghadir midget submarines were priority targets throughout the campaign, and the Pentagon has previously confirmed submarine kills by other means, including an MQ-9's Hellfire and an Army ATACMS strike.

The Black Aces were not alone. A VMFA-314 F-35C "Black Knights" jet returned with its own battle markings: an oil tanker, three submarines, a surface combatant, a Shahed-type drone, artillery, and launcher silhouettes, with tally marks beside AIM-120, AGM-154, GBU-31, GBU-54, and GBU-32 silhouettes.

For scale: the entire Eisenhower strike group fired 770 munitions across eight months of Red Sea fighting in 2023-2024. One squadron fired 421 in about two. The Pentagon has released relatively little official data on Epic Fury's ordnance expenditure — which is precisely why a squadron scoreboard photographed by a civilian spotter became news. It is worth stating plainly: the 421 figure comes from that photograph, not from a Navy release.

germany-f125-frigates-iris-t-missiles.content:
Germany is finally giving its biggest warships real air defenses. On Oct. 2, 2026, Diehl Defence and the federal procurement office BAAINBw signed an adaptation development contract to fit the naval version of the IRIS-T SLM surface-to-air missile to the German Navy's four F125 frigates — nine days after the Bundestag's budget committee approved the program on Sept. 23.

Each 7,200-ton frigate will receive two deck-mounted launchers holding 16 missiles apiece: 32 interceptors per ship, in vertical-launch canisters, against aircraft, helicopters, cruise missiles, and drones. The missile reaches 40 kilometers out and 20 kilometers up, guided by datalink with terminal self-homing.

The four ships of the Baden-Württemberg class — Baden-Württemberg, Nordrhein-Westfalen, Sachsen-Anhalt, Rheinland-Pfalz — were built for stabilization and crisis-management missions, and their armament showed it: short-range anti-ship missiles and two RIM-116 RAM point-defense launchers on a hull the size of a destroyer. The gap became a public embarrassment in 2024, when Baden-Württemberg detoured around Africa rather than transit the Red Sea on its return from an Indo-Pacific deployment.

## From concept to firing in ten months

The program is moving fast because the hard part is already done. In October 2025, during a naval firing exercise off Norway, engineers bolted a demonstrator launcher to the C-deck of Baden-Württemberg and engaged multiple targets using the ship's own radar data — going from concept to live firing in under ten months.

The naval adaptation strips out the ground system's support legs and hydraulics to save weight and deck space. Functional prototypes are expected in 2027, with sea trials and the first operational test launches the same year.


Diehl's own description of the goal is deliberately modest: "The aim is to make the system mission-capable on the German Navy's F125 frigates." But the engineering is not trivial. The naval IRIS-T SLM drops the ground launcher's support legs and hydraulics, fires from a compact vertical canister, and stays in contact with the ship via datalink until its own seeker takes over for the terminal phase — a fire-and-update architecture built for saturation attacks by drones and sea-skimmers.

## A missile with a combat record

The IRIS-T SLM is not a paper missile. German-supplied batteries in Ukraine have intercepted Shahed drones and Kh-101 and Kalibr cruise missiles at ranges up to 40 kilometers, and Berlin has explicitly cited that operational record in justifying the frigate upgrade.

The move fits Germany's broader post-2022 naval rearmament — new F126 frigates and Type 212CD submarines with Norway are in the pipeline alongside missile upgrades across the fleet. But the F125 fix is the most symbolically loaded: the ships were designed in an era when Berlin assumed its navy would police crises, not fight wars.

For a navy that watched its F124 frigate Hessen swat Houthi drones over the Red Sea under the EU's Operation Aspides while its newest, largest frigates lacked comparable defenses, the contract closes what The War Zone called one of the most conspicuous weaknesses in a Western fleet. Thirty-two missiles per ship will not make the F125 an air-defense destroyer. But it will, at last, give it teeth.

red-tails-f35-tuskegee-thunder-training.content:
For three days in mid-August, Dannelly Field in Montgomery, Alabama, became a war zone — simulated, but only just.

Operation Tuskegee Thunder, held Aug. 12-14, 2026, put the Alabama Air National Guard's 187th Fighter Wing through its paces in a scenario built around a Pacific operating environment. Airmen generated F-35A combat sorties while absorbing simulated attacks, degraded communications, chemical threats, drone incursions, casualties, gate runners, and mass-casualty drills — falling back on alternate and contingency command-and-control methods when their primary networks went down.

The exercise ran in conjunction with the wing's Combat Readiness Inspection, the formal evaluation of whether the Red Tails can generate and sustain combat airpower as part of the total force. For a wing that received its first F-35As in December 2023, transitioning from the F-16, it was the most important milestone of the conversion to date.

## "The entire wing has to be part of the fight"

"The F-35 is the most capable fighter aircraft in the world, but readiness is ultimately measured by our airmen's ability to fight and sustain operations in the most challenging conditions," said Col. John D. Caldwell, the wing's commander. "Operation Tuskegee Thunder provided our airmen the opportunity to hone their skills, refine tactics, techniques and procedures, and develop the confidence to operate anywhere, at any time."

Lt. Col. Martin "Lefty" Smith, an F-35 pilot who leads the wing's plans and programs, put the challenge in practical terms: operating a fifth-generation fighter in a contested environment requires the entire wing to be part of the fight — maintaining command and control, protecting and sustaining the force, adapting when the environment changes, and continuing to generate combat airpower. The challenge, he said, isn't simply launching aircraft.

## The inspection that matters

A Combat Readiness Inspection is the Air Force's periodic deep audit of a wing's ability to do its wartime job — not just fly, but deploy, communicate, protect, and sustain under pressure. For the 187th, passing through it with the F-35 validates years of conversion work: large-force exercises, night operations, and distributed training since the first Lightnings arrived at Dannelly Field.

The August inspection tested whether all of it holds together when the radios go down and the casualties start coming in — the unglamorous half of airpower, and the half that decides wars. The official releases describe what was tested, not how the wing scored; no outcome has been published.


The wing's path to the Lightning was a long one. The 187th flew the F-16 for decades before the first F-35As touched down at Dannelly Field in December 2023. Since then the conversion has run through the standard syllabus of a fighter wing changing airframes: large-force exercises to learn to fight as a package, night operations, and distributed training away from home station. Tuskegee Thunder was the exam that asked whether the wing could do all of it while someone was shooting back — at least on paper.

## A name with history

The Red Tails name honors the Tuskegee Airmen of World War II, the Black fighter pilots whose escort missions over Europe became legend. The 187th has carried that lineage through the F-16 era and into the F-35, and the exercise's name was no accident: Tuskegee Thunder was as much about heritage as readiness.
